content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Six checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Runs automatically after the
Sunday 02:30 adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Full memlint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural memlint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# Baylor Performance Clinic Joint Presentation (Eric + Jeremy Deck)

The Baylor Performance Clinic joint presentation is a co-authored slide deck delivered by Eric Rash and Jeremy Frazier for a Friday clinic (~July 2026). On 2026-07-09, Eric's updated opening/closing content (produced 7/6) was merged into the shared deck against Jeremy's 7/6 middle-section revisions, producing `UPDATED_Clinic_Presentation_v2.pptx` (31 slides) on the Desktop\DEV directory. The session resolved a merge gap in which Eric's bookend sections predated Jeremy's most recent middle-section edits, and re-established a clean speaker handoff structure across the three-part deck.

## Key Points

- **Three-part handoff structure:** Eric opens slides 1–10, Jeremy runs 11–22, Eric closes 23–31. Jeremy's middle section (his 7/6 edits, S9–20 in his source) was preserved byte-for-byte untouched during the merge — only Eric's bookend sections were modified.
- **v2 file convention:** the merged result was saved as `UPDATED_Clinic_Presentation_v2.pptx` (31 slides) leaving the original `UPDATED_Clinic_Presentation.pptx` untouched, per Eric's explicit request. This mirrors the "clean backup alongside the working file" delivery pattern seen in other deliverables.
- **Merged content additions:** S5 SL Broad Jump ("act when ~10% short" + LSI phase-gate caption), S6 rebuilt (CMJ RSI + football 5-10-5 decel example), new S7 "More rosters. Same method." (repeat-sprint asymmetry, volleyball/basketball approach-jump trend), new S8 "The camera you already own." video slide, S30 QR-card "Take both home right now" rewrite.
- **Footer renumbering:** footers were non-sequential leftovers from three merged source decks; they were renumbered 01–31 sequentially. Stale speaker notes ("Close Part One / hand off") were rewritten to match the new structure.
- **Bash tool failure → PowerShell:** the Bash tool misbehaved with silent exit-1 errors during pptx work; switching to PowerShell succeeded. Visual verification via PowerPoint export/render caught three text-overflow issues on the new slides.

## Details

The core merge challenge was a version desynchronization across a collaboratively-authored deck. Jeremy modified the middle section (S9–20) the morning of 2026-07-09 — rewording "The Shared Goal," moving Objective Measures earlier, rewriting Healing/Foundation phase questions with tech-vs-field splits, relocating Resource-Limited Settings to S17, and deleting the five-test Field Battery slide. Eric's opening and closing sections, by contrast, predated the 7/6 update cycle. The merge reconciled these by treating Jeremy's section as authoritative and immutable (copied byte-for-byte) while updating only Eric's bookend content, avoiding any risk of clobbering a collaborator's recent work. This "one author owns each contiguous slide range, never edit across the boundary" discipline is the presentation analog of the untracked-files and mirror-file cautions seen elsewhere in collaborative work.

Two verification lessons emerged. First, programmatic pptx editing benefits from a visual render pass: exporting/rendering the deck in PowerPoint caught three text-overflow issues on newly-authored slides that were invisible at the XML/tooling layer — a direct instance of the "verify directly, don't trust the intermediate layer" principle. Second, the Bash tool's silent exit-1 failures during pptx manipulation on Windows required falling back to PowerShell, a recurring cross-tool substitution pattern. Three open items remained: the QR code is still dead pending Eric manually setting the Drive folder link-sharing to "anyone with the link can view" (not achievable via tooling); the QR card replaced an old "Resource" card citing Mark Jamison's *"Rethinking Return to Play"* (if Jeremy wants it kept, the PDF must be dropped into the Drive folder); and slide 10's "Full Circle / Better Process. Better Outcomes." ladder needs verification with Jeremy because its speaker note reads like closing-callback language, suggesting a possible misplacement from an earlier merge.

# Session Context Footprint Audit (doctor-plus)

On 2026-08-15, a `doctor-plus` context-engineering audit was run against the Claude Code environment and rendered as a standalone HTML report. The audit returned 3 FLAG / 3 PASS across six "then-and-now" context-engineering shifts. Its core numeric finding is that **approximately 21,500 tokens are always loaded at session start, versus the ~3,000 that `CLAUDE.md` claims for itself** — a roughly 7× gap between the documented and measured standing footprint.

## Key Points

- **~21.5k tokens always loaded at session start** versus a stated ~3,000 in `CLAUDE.md`. The ~7,640-token floor (guidance files plus memory-compiler injection) is directly measured; the skill-description totals that make up the remainder are approximate.
- **The audit modified nothing.** No workspace files were changed by the audit run, and the report footer records this explicitly — a read-only diagnostic whose output is a document, not an edit.
- **Delivered as a local self-contained file** (`~/Desktop/doctor-plus-report.html`, 23.7 KB) with zero external resources: no CDN, no network calls. It therefore works offline and survives being emailed or moved, unlike a published artifact link.
- **Self-review of the generated CSS caught three malformed hex values inside the dark-theme block** before the file was opened. Color declarations that live only inside `@media` or `[data-theme]` blocks are the classic source of the unreadable-artifact bug, because they are invisible in the default rendering path.
- **Pre-flight checks that paid off:** tag balance; every CSS variable used is defined in the bare `:root` (verified correct in all three theme states — light, dark, and unstamped system default); zero external resources; stacked-bar segments summing to exactly 100%.
- **A single scaled stacked bar with a dashed marker at the claimed 3,000-token budget** made the stated-versus-measured gap legible at a glance, replacing a table the reader would otherwise have to parse.

## Details

The audit's substantive finding is a measurement discipline problem rather than a bug: `CLAUDE.md` carries a self-description of its own token cost that has gone stale as the environment grew, and nothing in the system reconciles the stated figure against the measured one. The ~7,640-token floor from guidance files and memory-compiler injection is the reliably measurable part; the balance up to ~21.5k comes from skill descriptions, which is the same budget quantified independently at 71,248 characters across 150 skills in [[concepts/skill-description-budget-ceiling]]. The two findings corroborate each other from different directions — one counts characters in the skills repo, the other counts tokens at session start — and together they identify skill descriptions as the dominant term in standing context cost. Reconciling the stale ~3,000 figure in `CLAUDE.md` was left as an open question.

The report's construction contributes a reusable set of pre-flight checks for generated HTML artifacts. The most valuable is the theme-block scan: three malformed hex values were sitting inside the dark-theme block, where they would not appear in a light-mode preview and would only surface for a reader whose system was set to dark. Verifying that every CSS variable referenced is also defined in the bare `:root` — not merely inside a theme block — closes the related gap where an unstamped system default renders with undefined variables. Checking all three theme states (light, dark, unstamped default) rather than the one the author happens to be using is the generalizable rule, and it is the same "check the non-default viewport" discipline that surfaced the slide-8 chart overflow and slide-11 dark-background bugs in [[concepts/athlete-monitoring-rtp-presentation]].

The delivery and design choices were made against the report's purpose. A local self-contained file with zero external resources was chosen over a published artifact specifically so the document survives being moved or emailed and functions offline; publishing as a shareable link was offered as an addition rather than a replacement. The visual treatment was deliberately utilitarian — an "instrument report" rather than an editorial one — with cool blue-biased ink on cool off-white, a serif display face over system sans body text, and monospaced tabular numerals throughout, on the reasoning that the report's entire argument is numeric and figures must align for comparison. PASS/FLAG states were encoded as pine and burnt-amber pills held deliberately separate from the slate-blue accent color, so that semantic state does not read as branding. The 1–6 shift numbering was retained only because those numbers are real identifiers from the source article; numbering that carries information is kept, numbering that decorates is not. The single scaled stacked bar with a dashed marker at the claimed 3,000-token budget is the report's central device: it converts a two-number comparison that a table would force the reader to compute into a proportion visible immediately.

# Connection: Pick the Ground-Truth Check That Matches the Layer That's Lying

## The Connection

[[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] generalizes a rule from two 2026-04-22 sessions: when a tool's output looks plausible but can't be double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive check — raw PDF text instead of an agent's summary, `file://` rendering instead of a preview server. [[concepts/claude-code-worktree-gotchas]] documents the CRLF/`autocrlf` gotcha, where `git status`, shell `==`, and diff tools all report two files as different when the stored blobs are byte-identical, and where the reliable check is `git hash-object` (or `xxd` / `Format-Hex` / `cat -A`) rather than anything that reads the working-tree representation.

These are the same discipline, but the CRLF case runs the failure in the opposite direction, and that inversion is what makes the pairing worth writing down.

## Key Points

- The 04-22 cases are **false negatives of suspicion**: the surface said "fine" (a plausible author list, a correct relative path) when something was wrong or unverifiable. The CRLF case is a **false positive**: the surface said "different" when nothing was wrong at all.
- Both are resolved by the same move — bypass the intermediate representation — but "more primitive" is not a single direction. You have to know *which* layer is transforming the data before you know what counts as ground truth.
- For Git on Windows the transforming layer is the checkout filter, so ground truth is the object store (`git hash-object`, which hashes the post-normalization blob), not the bytes on disk. For a preview server the transforming layer is the renderer, so ground truth is the file opened directly. For an agent the transforming layer is summarization, so ground truth is the source document.
- A false-positive difference is more expensive than a false-negative one, because it invites you to "fix" content that was never broken. The `git update-index --refresh` resolution works precisely because it changes the index's belief, not any file.
- Corollary for scripts: the pre-commit `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` divergence hook in [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]] must compare `git hash-object` output, not working-tree bytes — a comparison written against the wrong layer will fire spuriously forever on one platform and never on another.

## Details

The verify-before-trusting rule as originally stated is asymmetric: it assumes the risk is *accepting* bad output. Both 2026-04-22 evidence items fit that shape — the hallucinated citations for IDs 286/287/358 would have been committed, and the missing photo would have been "fixed" by rewriting correct HTML. The remedy in both cases was to find a channel with fewer transformations between the artifact and the observer.

The worktree gotchas article supplies the missing half of the rule. On a Windows checkout with `core.autocrlf = true`, every tracked text file is transformed on the way out of the object store and on the way back in. Any tool that reads the working tree — `git status`, a shell string comparison, a diff viewer — is reading a *derived* representation, and after a branch switch or IDE restart the index's cached stat data can disagree with that derivation even though no content changed. The result is a phantom modification: a difference that exists only in the reporting layer. Stepping down here does not mean reading raw bytes off disk, because the raw bytes on disk are exactly the thing that has been transformed; it means asking Git what blob it would store, via `git hash-object`. Naively applying "get closer to the metal" — running `xxd` on both files and comparing — would confirm the difference and confirm the wrong conclusion.

So the transferable formulation is narrower and more useful than "verify directly." It is: **identify the layer performing the transformation, then choose a check on the far side of it.** Sometimes the far side is more primitive (raw PDF text under an agent's summary). Sometimes it is more abstract (the canonical blob hash above the platform-mangled working tree). The 04-22 sessions happened to hit two cases where primitive and correct coincided, which is why the rule was written as "step down." The CRLF case shows that direction is incidental. This also explains why `git update-index --refresh` is the right fix rather than touching files: once you know the discrepancy lives in the index's view and not in the content, the correct repair is to the view.

The same reasoning covers the third gotcha in that article, though less directly. A `git worktree add` failure caused by Windows MAX_PATH reports as a checkout error on the file being written, which invites debugging the change in flight; the actual cause is pre-existing repo content in `SourcePapers/`. The error surface names the wrong layer, and the fix — sparse-checkout, or disabling background isolation — only becomes visible once you stop trusting the layer that reported the failure.

## Related Concepts

- [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] — The original "step down to a more primitive check" rule from the 2026-04-22 citation-hallucination and preview-server sessions.
- [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]] — The dual-context pre-commit sync hook whose file comparison is directly exposed to this layer-selection choice.

- [[concepts/accidental-git-init-home-directory]] — Another case where a git tool's surface output diverges from what is actually stored.

# Skylar Zinnecker CMJ Return-to-Competition Reports

A series of CMJ (countermovement jump) force-plate performance reports were built for Baylor Athletics athlete Skylar Zinnecker on 2026-04-14, to support a return-to-competition (RTC) decision following injury and surgery. The reports were delivered as polished, print-ready HTML files using Chart.js, and were followed by a terminology cleanup and project documentation pass.

## Key Points

- Source data was a VALD ForceDecks export (`CMJ-test-export-04_14_2026.csv`, 67 sessions spanning August 2023-April 2026), processed into HTML reports with Chart.js visualizations.
- Injury (April 12, 2025) and surgery (April 25, 2025) dates were annotated as vertical markers on the charts.
- The baseline was redefined from a full 2-year historical average to the last 4 pre-injury sessions (March 20-April 10, 2025) - a clinically more appropriate baseline for an RTC assessment - while "current" values used a 3-session rolling average from April 2, 7, and 8, 2026.
- The baseline change flipped the Lower-Limb Stiffness metric's status from "Progressing" (⚠) to "Exceeds Baseline" (✓), since the new baseline (4,693) was lower than the old one (5,477); asymmetry metrics were normalized inversely (lower % = better) for the radar chart.
- The term "nadir"/"Injury Nadir" (the post-surgery performance floor used in the recovery-percentage formula) was replaced with the clinically clearer "Post-Op Low" across all three HTML files (9 instances total), after the user found "nadir" too jargon-heavy for a clinical audience.

## Details

Styling followed Baylor's institutional branding (`#1e4d2b` green, `#b87d0a` gold) in light mode, with full print CSS (`@page` set to letter portrait, plus `-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact` to preserve colors when printed). The athlete portrait (`SZ.jpg`) was referenced via a relative path rather than embedded as base64, meaning the image and HTML files must be kept in the same directory for the reports to render correctly.

Several practical lessons emerged during the build. The `Edit` tool fails outright if its `old_string` argument doesn't match the file exactly, so the working pattern became: use `Grep` to confirm the exact existing text, re-read the surrounding context, and only then call `Edit`. A PowerShell image-dimension check required `Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Drawing` to be loaded before `[System.Drawing.Image]` could be used. Duplicate JS object keys (e.g., in a color palette) can silently survive an `Edit`, so any palette change was verified afterward with `Grep`. After all six requested deliverables were completed and saved to `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\SpecialRequests\Zinnecker_Skylar\`, a follow-up session ran `/init` to generate `CLAUDE.md` and `session_notes.md`, documenting the project for any future session that picks it back up.

# End-of-Day Structured Interview Workflow

A structured end-of-day interview workflow was demonstrated on 2026-05-29, combining a Fireflies meeting sync, a 4-question daily debrief, targeted vault note creation, and global memory system updates (USER.md and MEMORY.md). The session also revealed a critical USER.md character cap constraint and clarified the Tier A vs. Tier B memory split for active vs. durable information.

## Key Points

- **4-question interview format** covers all active projects and workstreams in a single pass, surfacing insights across areas that might otherwise receive no end-of-day attention. The 2026-05-29 run spanned: Dropback vendor call, Jeremy presentation prep, Hoff/Soto AI discovery call, ACWR tennis project, Fall Camp simulator scoping, spirit and cheer summer packet, research database, and upcoming Databricks call.
- **Q4 ("tell a peer one thing") consistently produces the sharpest material:** this prompt forces compression — the user must identify the single transmissible insight from the day. On 2026-05-29 it surfaced: "effort put into answering questions that haven't been asked is in vain" (essay seed), and the connected observation that AI adoption/consensus is the real bottleneck, not direction.
- **Connect interview outputs to existing vault notes rather than creating isolated ones:** updating the existing `self-authored-direction` note with a reframed open question (linking direction to adoption) compounds value more than creating a standalone new note. The connection is the knowledge, not just the content.
- **USER.md cap (1,375 chars):** the global USER.md profile is essentially at capacity (1,370/1,375 as of 2026-05-29). Any future profile addition requires consolidating or pruning existing entries before adding new content — USER.md must be treated as a fixed-size buffer, not an append-only log.
- **MEMORY.md Tier A vs. Tier B:** durable facts about the user go in Tier A; active, fluid threads (e.g., career-pivot consideration) go in Tier B. A Tier B entry signals "this is worth tracking but not yet stable enough to become a fact."
- **Fireflies integration:** new meetings are synced, renamed from generic timestamps to descriptive titles (e.g., `2026-05-28_Eric_and_Jeremy_presentation_prep`), and exported to the vault at `Inbox/meetings/YYYY-MM-DD_<title>.md`.

## Details

The structured end-of-day interview functions as a compression mechanism: a full day of meetings, decisions, and half-formed thoughts is distilled into a small set of high-signal outputs — a vault note, a memory update, an essay seed — without requiring the user to decide in the moment what is worth capturing. By following a fixed question format, the interview ensures consistent coverage across all active workstreams rather than capturing only what was most recent or most emotionally salient. The structure also makes the interview reproducible across sessions and assistants: the same prompt set can be run by any AI instance with access to the user's project context and yield comparable coverage.

The Q4 prompt is architecturally different from the preceding questions because it forces a different cognitive operation. Questions 1–3 surface facts and status updates (what happened, what decisions were made, what is blocked); Q4 forces synthesis and compression — the user must identify the single insight worth transmitting to a peer. This compression step often reveals insights that would not have surfaced through status-update prompts alone. On 2026-05-29, both outputs from Q4 were routed to vault notes rather than MEMORY.md, because they are essay seeds and framing questions rather than durable facts about the user's preferences or context. The distinction matters: MEMORY.md stores facts that help a future AI session orient quickly ("user works at Baylor Athletics"), while vault notes store ideas that the user may want to develop, publish, or return to. AI-adoption/consensus was explicitly deferred to the weekly review rather than drafted immediately — the weekly review is the right context for framing the evidence, finding allies, and deciding whether the idea is worth writing.

- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] — The three-tier memory architecture (native auto-memory, Stop-hook scratchpad, claude-memory-compiler) that the USER.md/MEMORY.md system extends; the Tier A/Tier B distinction in MEMORY.md maps to a similar "durable vs. active" split.
- [[connections/obsidian-vault-as-knowledge-hub]] — The Fireflies meeting export and interview-derived vault note creation are further instances of routing structured outputs to the SecondBrain vault as a canonical knowledge destination.
- [[concepts/project-triage-retrospective]] — The end-of-day interview provides day-level compression; the weekly retrospective provides week-level triage across cold projects and open loops. The two complement each other at different time horizons.

# Porting Skills from claude.ai Web UI to Local ~/.claude/skills/

On 2026-05-28, eight personal skills authored in the claude.ai web UI were ported to the local `~/.claude/skills/` directory for use inside Claude Code. Because the web UI does not provide a bulk export mechanism, skills were extracted individually via Playwright browser automation. Only the `SKILL.md` content is recoverable from the web UI — supporting files (scripts, reference templates, JSON schemas) are not downloadable and must be recreated separately.

## Key Points

- **Extraction method:** navigate to `claude.ai/customize/skills`, click each skill, toggle the "Code view" control, then extract the raw markdown from the line containers — Playwright automates this sequence reliably.
- **Eight skills ported (2026-05-28):** `starter-design-tokens`, `starter-icp-positioning`, `starter-voice-profile`, `five-slides-generator`, `articulation-skill`, `skill-evaluator`, `pbir-report-builder`, `everything-search`. Two web-UI skills were skipped — `skill-creator` and `mcp-builder` — because local plugin versions already covered their functionality.
- **Supporting files are not recoverable from the web UI:** `pbir-report-builder/references/json-templates/*`, `skill-evaluator/scripts/*.py`, and `everything-search/scripts/search.py` are referenced in the corresponding `SKILL.md` files but are not accessible through the web UI scrape. These files must be recreated from scratch if running the skills locally.
- **Naming collision strategy:** use a `-web` suffix on skills whose name conflicts with an existing local skill (e.g., `five-slides-generator-web`). No conflicts occurred in the 2026-05-28 batch.
- **Keep references lean:** skill reference directories should contain only files that `SKILL.md` actually cites. Binary formats (`.pptx`, `.docx`) were explicitly excluded — `5_Sides_Content_Templates.docx` was converted to a lean `talking-points.md` extracting only the timing budget and speaker-note structure, discarding social-post and video-script templates as out-of-scope for the slide skill.
- **Research-intent skills must not include finished examples:** skills designed to conduct fresh research ("every statistic from web search") should not reference completed example outputs as supporting files — doing so undermines the design intent by biasing the model toward lifting from the example rather than researching anew.
- **Marp as optional parallel format:** the `five-slides-generator` skill was enhanced to offer Marp markdown output as an optional Step 8 format alongside the existing pptxgenjs path. The VS Code Marp extension (not the Marp CLI) is sufficient for preview and export (HTML/PDF/PPTX) via the command palette — the CLI is unnecessary when the extension is installed.

## Details

The web UI extraction process works because claude.ai's `/customize/skills` page renders each skill's raw SKILL.md content in a "Code view" that can be read by Playwright's DOM traversal. The workflow is: authenticate to claude.ai in a Playwright-controlled browser, navigate to `/customize/skills`, click each skill tile to expand it, toggle "Code view" on, and collect the text from the code block. This approach is fragile against UI redesigns but reliable against the current claude.ai layout. The main practical limitation is that the extraction surfaces only the SKILL.md file — any companion files in a skill's `scripts/` or `references/` subdirectory exist only on the claude.ai server and are not served to the client during the Code view render.

For skills whose supporting files are missing after a port, the correct recovery strategy is to recreate them from the SKILL.md's instructions and examples rather than attempting any other extraction path. In practice, SKILL.md files written for the web UI are often self-contained enough that the skill functions adequately without the supporting files, but skills with heavy template or script dependencies (e.g., `pbir-report-builder` needing JSON schema templates, or `skill-evaluator` needing its Python scoring scripts) will produce degraded output or fail outright until the files are recreated. Recording which skills have missing dependencies — as action items in the daily log — is the recommended approach so the gap is not silently forgotten.

The decision to convert `.docx` to `.md` for the five-slides-generator's talking-points reference illustrates a broader principle for skill reference management: binary formats introduce format friction (requiring additional tools to read), risk content-lifting over fresh research, and are harder to diff and review in version control. Extracting only the semantically durable structure (timing budget + speaker-note conventions) from the `.docx` into a lean markdown file produced a reference that is both smaller and more useful for the skill's actual purpose.

# KeystoneOS Repo Intake Flow (inventory → intake → promote)

The KeystoneOS repo intake flow is the AGENTS.md-defined three-stage pipeline — `inventory` → `intake` → `promote` — for discovering repositories across configured discovery roots and registering genuinely new ones in the KeystoneOS project registry. On 2026-07-13, a run scanned 58 candidates (14 already registered), promoted two genuinely new repos as "Active candidate," left 17 low-signal items in the review bucket, and committed the registry update under standing auto-commit authorization.

## Key Points

- **Three-stage flow:** `inventory` scans discovery roots for candidate repos; `intake` scores and buckets candidates, writing a report (`outputs/intake/2026-07-08-project-intake.md`); `promote` registers selected candidates in the registry. Each item in the intake report carries its own recommended promote command.
- **2026-07-13 results:** 58 candidates scanned, 14 already registered; two new repos promoted — `cmj_traffic_light` (CMJ recovery monitoring for Volleyball, 4 commits, registered at its OneDrive work-drive path as its only home) and `PlayerProfiles_FB_03_28_2026` (football player profiles with Perch API ingest, 43 commits, registered at canonical `DEV\` path). 17 low-signal items left unpromoted in the review bucket.
- **DEV is canonical; skip OneDrive shadows:** OneDrive INBOX copies of Travel_Map, ForcePlate_DecisionSystem, and PlayerProfiles were skipped as shadows of already-registered DEV repos, per drive-topology policy. A repo whose only home is OneDrive (cmj_traffic_light) is registered at that path; a repo with a canonical DEV copy is registered there and its OneDrive duplicate ignored.
- **Ambiguous scope flagged, not assumed:** the user's "new repo ingestion" phrasing was interpreted as discover-and-register-all-new, but the assistant flagged the assumption and offered to promote specific review-bucket repos instead if that was the intent.
- **JSON schema and PowerShell gotchas:** the intake report's JSON schemas differed from initial assumptions — inspect shapes before parsing and use the report's own recommended promote commands. PowerShell `Select-Object` clipped formatted `keystone.ps1 health` output; rerun `health` plain rather than piping through `Select-Object`.

## Details

The intake flow operationalizes the earlier DEV-sweep classification model (see [[concepts/keystoneos-project-registry]]) as a repeatable, command-driven pipeline. Where the DEV sweep bucketed projects into confirmed-live / ambiguous / inactive, the intake flow produces a scored candidate report and registers only genuinely new, sufficiently-signaled repos as "Active candidate," leaving low-signal items in a review bucket for explicit user decision. The conservatism is the same: ambiguous or low-signal repos are never auto-promoted, and the run flagged its own interpretation of an ambiguous user instruction rather than proceeding silently. The two promotions on 2026-07-13 illustrate the drive-topology policy in action — `cmj_traffic_light` was registered at its OneDrive path because that is its only home, while `PlayerProfiles_FB_03_28_2026` was registered at its canonical `DEV\` path and its OneDrive INBOX duplicate skipped, consistent with the rule that DEV is canonical and OneDrive copies are shadows.

Two operational gotchas surfaced. First, the intake report's JSON output did not match the shapes initially assumed for parsing; the correct practice is to inspect the actual JSON structure before writing parse logic and to use each item's own recommended promote command rather than reconstructing commands independently. Second, piping the formatted output of `keystone.ps1 health` through PowerShell's `Select-Object` clipped the display — a rendering artifact of PowerShell's formatted-object pipeline rather than a data problem — so the reliable path is to rerun `health` plain without the pipe. The registry update was committed and pushed to main (`7140ad1`) under the KeystoneOS repo's standing auto-commit authorization, and review-bucket candidates (e.g., AT_Utilization_Benchmarks, baylor-gps-football) remain unpromoted pending user direction.

# ~/DEV Knowledge Graph Refresh (185 → 2,190 Files)

On 2026-09-01 the stale April graphify build of `~/DEV` (185 files) was rebuilt against the current 2,190-file corpus, with Codex running independent verification passes over the artifact. The session finalized at 9,256 nodes, 18,341 edges, and 628 named communities at `~/DEV/graphify-out/graph.html`, with zero correctness defects and zero regressions per Codex, but with completeness deliberately left incomplete: 1,099 files and 95 of 130 converted office documents remain unextracted, blocked by the Gemini free-tier daily quota. Resume instructions live in `~/DEV/graphify-out/RESUME.md`.

## Key Points

- **Chunk size drives extraction yield nonlinearly:** 60 files per chunk yielded 17%, 20 files yielded ~38%, and 15 files yielded 100%. `GF_CHUNK=15` is the settled value; the resume command is `GF_CHUNK=15 ~/DEV/graphify-out/scripts/office_loop.sh 25 6`.
- **Gemini free tier enforces two independent caps** — 5 requests/minute *and* 20/day per model. The per-minute cap is the operative bottleneck because each request burns roughly 5 minutes in backoff; the daily cap was confirmed *not* to reset at midnight during a post-midnight retry.
- **Rebuild the graph after every extraction pass.** A graph built at 20:55 was shipped alongside a Gemini extraction layer written at 01:22, so 0 of 256 Gemini nodes appeared in the artifact. The merge code was correct — it had simply never been re-run against the newer layer.
- **Five real defects found across the passes:** the missing graph layer above; a scope filter silently dropping all 130 office docs (they convert to `.md` *inside* an excluded folder); one minified vendor file producing 650 junk nodes and 3,699 junk edges; zero-yield files marked "done" so they would never retry (221 requeued); and an omitted `root=` argument collapsing paths to basenames and zeroing attribution.
- **Long-running extraction must checkpoint.** Save-at-the-end meant a 10-minute foreground timeout wiped an entire pass; checkpointing now happens every 30 files. Background jobs were separately killed externally twice — background execution is not a safety guarantee for long jobs.

## Details

The dominant technical finding is the chunk-size/yield relationship, which is steep enough to change the shape of the job rather than just its speed. Moving from 60 to 15 files per chunk took extraction yield from 17% to 100%, meaning larger chunks were not merely slower but were silently discarding the majority of their input. Combined with the Gemini free tier's 5-requests-per-minute ceiling — which converts each request into roughly five minutes of wall-clock backoff — the extraction leg is fundamentally a slow, quota-metered pipeline whose throughput cannot be improved by batching harder. That constraint is what forced the session's central decision: after three consecutive failures (two external background-job kills and a foreground rate-limit wall), work stopped and the graph was finalized with the state on hand rather than burning further attempts against a quota that a post-midnight retry proved had not reset.

The stale-layer bug is the most instructive of the five defects because nothing in the pipeline reported an error. The graph artifact was built before its own newest input existed, so a correct merge implementation produced an artifact missing 256 nodes while every component reported success. This is the same shape as the manifest-omission class in [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]]: the executed steps all succeeded, and the defect lives entirely in what was never included. The scope filter dropping all 130 office docs has the same character — the conversion step wrote `.md` outputs into a folder the extractor excluded, so a hundred-plus documents disappeared between two individually-correct stages. The operational rule the session settled on, "rebuild the graph and re-export HTML after every extraction pass, then re-run Codex verification before calling it done," exists precisely because per-stage success does not compose into artifact correctness.

Two process lessons carry beyond graphify. First, scripts living in the job scratch folder die with the job — a trap already flagged in the user's own notes and repeated here; all 15 scripts were relocated to `~/DEV/graphify-out/scripts/` and shell wrappers repointed, since the wrappers still held stale scratch paths. The Codex verification reports were likewise copied out of the disposable scratch folder into `~/DEV/graphify-out/` so the handoff document would reference durable paths. Second, when the user caught a logging bug that printed `0 nodes` while nodes actually existed, the discrepancy was explained away rather than fixed — recorded as an explicit instruction to push to fix rather than rationalize. A handoff document was written for resumption in another session, secret-scanned clean with all referenced paths verified, though it was placed in a `/var/folders/.../T/` temp path. Two open ARMS gaps noted in that handoff remain unaddressed.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

## Evidence

- 2026-04-22 (10:57): "Background agent produced `docs/batch_r7_fixes.json` but hallucinated wrong author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358... Used PyPDF2 text extraction to verify actual authors and corrected all three citations before committing."
- 2026-04-22 (17:21): "Photo failed to render in localhost preview — identified as a server limitation (brainstorm preview server doesn't serve image files), not an HTML error... always verify photo rendering by opening the HTML directly in Chrome via file:// URL."

# Athlete Monitoring / Return-to-Play Conference Presentation Design

On 2026-06-17, a conference presentation slide deck (~20-min talk) was designed for a visually-oriented sports science audience covering athlete monitoring and return-to-play data workflows. The design process resolved four key architectural decisions — framing, statistical thresholds, content constraints, and audience philosophy — and produced a locked 11-slide running order built around a single-athlete RTP narrative with minimal text and strong visual anchors. A subsequent validation pass confirmed all slides were layout-clean and fixed a dark-mode visibility bug on the final slide. On 2026-06-18, a full speaker script was written for the deck (`RTP-Data-Collection-SCRIPT.md`), a duration analysis showed the 11-slide deck ran far short of its 20-minute slot, and the deck was expanded to 14 slides (v2) with v1 preserved.

## Key Points

- **Single-athlete framing throughout:** roster-comparison views were explicitly rejected as "off-topic for the individual RTP framing." The presentation's decision-support narrative only holds together when the audience follows one athlete's trajectory from injury through return-to-competition decisions. Adding a roster view introduces a different clinical use case that fragments narrative coherence.
- **Visual-first audience philosophy:** the intended audience "eats with their eyes" — conversational delivery carries the explanatory load while slides provide visual anchors, not text. Minimal text per slide; strong imagery and color-coded indicators are the design primitives.
- **Z-score traffic-light thresholds: −1.5 SD / −2 SD.** Applied in the Excel demo to translate raw metrics into actionable status flags. −1.5 SD = caution/yellow; −2 SD = concern/red. The leave-behind template implements the same logic, ensuring the presentation and the artifact practitioners actually use share the same statistical foundation.
- **Screenshots-only (no live build):** consistent with the leave-behind template format. All data visualization examples appear as screenshots rather than live-built charts, eliminating technical failure risk in a conference setting.
- **11-slide running order:** bridge → decision-first framing (×2) → generalizing → metric selection → blank template → populated/flagged → charted → stakeholder report → take-home materials → close.
- **Slide 9 — Sample Stakeholder Report:** single-athlete trend chart + color-coded status flag + one plain-language interpretive line. Models the exact artifact the audience would produce and deliver to coaching/medical staff, completing the "here is the workflow" → "here is the output" arc.
- **Josse referenced verbally only (not on-screen):** a named methodological reference was kept off slides for sensitivity reasons; verbal attribution suffices for academic credentialing without creating a circulating visual artifact.
- **Slide validation (Session 23:56):** All 11 slides confirmed layout-clean at 1440×900 and 375×667. Synthetic keyboard event dispatch (`keydown`) is unreliable for slide navigation in browser automation — smooth-scroll does not complete on synthetic key events in browser extension automation contexts. Use direct navigation-dot element clicks for reliable automated HTML slide deck validation.
- **Dark-background slides require adaptive nav chrome:** Slide 11 uses a dark background (`rgb(17,17,17)`); the default nav-dot and slide-counter colors (`rgba(0,0,0,0.45)`) are invisible against it. Fix: an `on-dark` CSS class toggled on `<body>` by the `setActive()` JavaScript function enables CSS overrides for nav elements on dark slides. This pattern generalizes to any HTML slide deck with alternating light/dark slide backgrounds.
- **A tight, purposeful deck runs far shorter than its slot (2026-06-18):** the 11-slide "You Have the Data. Now What?" deck at correct density runs ~5–7 minutes (7–9 with pauses), leaving an 11–14 minute gap against the 20-minute target. Closing the gap requires real content (case-study athlete walkthrough, live-demo narration for the data table and chart slides, planted audience Q&A), not padding — slide count and density are the drivers, not verbosity.
- **Speaker script + v1/v2 versioning (2026-06-18):** a full per-slide speaker script with talking points, notes, and pacing was saved to `outputs/presentation/RTP-Data-Collection-SCRIPT.md`. The deck was expanded to 14 slides; the original 11-slide version was reconstructed from git and preserved as `RTP-Data-Collection-v1.html`, the 14-slide version saved as `RTP-Data-Collection-v2.html`, with the working file `RTP-Data-Collection.html` aliasing v2. Preserving v1 before editing follows an "always keep the original" versioning discipline.
- **Slide 8 chart overflow fix (2026-06-18):** the slide-8 line chart overflowed at short/landscape viewports (~896×414); fixed with `aspect-ratio` plus `max-height: min(40vh, 320px)`. This is a second responsive-layout defect (alongside the slide-11 dark-theme fix) that only surfaced at non-standard viewport sizes, reinforcing multi-viewport render verification.

## Details

The presentation's core design challenge is bridging the gap between analytical rigor and practitioner legibility for a mixed audience of sports scientists, athletic trainers, and coaches. A talk that leads with methodology (sensor setup, reliability coefficients, statistical assumptions) loses practitioners in the first two minutes; a talk that shows only colored flags without any basis loses the sports scientists. The "decision-first framing (×2)" in the running order addresses this: the talk opens with the end product — the practitioner's decision — and only then traces backward to the analytical workflow that supports it. The repetition reinforces the framing before technical detail begins.

The z-score threshold design (−1.5 / −2 SD) was chosen for the Excel demo because it is transferable: any clinician working with any monitoring dataset can understand and apply standard deviation cutoffs without statistical training beyond "how far from the average." The traffic-light metaphor (green/yellow/red) maps intuitively to go/caution/stop decisions without requiring the audience to interpret numbers directly. The leave-behind template implements the same −1.5 / −2 SD thresholds automatically, so practitioners who use it after the session are working with the same statistical logic demonstrated in the talk — reducing drift toward arbitrary threshold modification post-session.

Slide 9's stakeholder report design was added specifically to address the "so what do I hand to the coach/AT?" question that sports scientists routinely face after building a monitoring pipeline. The three-element structure (trend chart + status flag + one interpretive sentence) is the minimum viable stakeholder report: more complex outputs tend to go unread or generate confusion when shared with coaching staff who do not routinely interpret data visualizations. The time budget for the talk was kept deliberately soft — enriching content depth was prioritized over strict adherence to 20 minutes, on the premise that a substantive overrun is less damaging than a rushed, thin presentation for an engaged sports science audience. The frontend-slides skill was loaded after all content decisions were locked to execute the build phase.

Following the content design session (20:28), a validation pass (Session 23:56) confirmed all 11 slides rendered correctly at both standard and mobile viewport sizes. The initial browser automation approach used synthetic keydown events to navigate between slides — this proved unreliable because the presentation's smooth-scroll transition does not complete when triggered by a synthetic key event in browser extension automation contexts. Switching to direct navigation-dot element clicks resolved this. A dark-mode visibility bug was discovered on Slide 11, whose dark background (`rgb(17,17,17)`) made both the slide counter text and the inactive navigation dots invisible in their default dark-gray color (`rgba(0,0,0,0.45)`). The fix uses a `setActive()` JavaScript function that toggles an `on-dark` class on the `<body>` element each time a new slide becomes active.

The 2026-06-18 work moved the deck from a validated visual artifact toward a delivery-ready talk. Writing the speaker script exposed a duration mismatch that the slide count alone had masked: a deck deliberately built for high visual density and low text runs quickly when narrated, so the 11-slide deck consumed only ~5–7 minutes of a 20-minute slot. The assistant explicitly declined to "pad" the existing script and instead framed three substance-based gap-closure paths (expand the script in place, add 4–6 slides, or a hybrid), identifying the data-table and chart slides, a case-study athlete walkthrough, and planted audience-participation moments as the highest-value additions. The deck was then expanded to 14 slides (v2), and the original 11-slide deck was reconstructed from git and preserved as v1 — an instance of keeping the prior version before making a structural edit. A second responsive defect was fixed during this pass: the slide-8 line chart overflowed at short landscape viewports and was constrained with `aspect-ratio` and a `max-height: min(40vh, 320px)` cap, echoing the slide-11 dark-theme fix as a layout bug invisible at the default viewport but present at edge sizes.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/skylar-zinnecker-cmj-rtc-reports]] — Individual RTC reports built from VALD ForceDecks data for a single athlete; shares the single-athlete framing, Baylor institutional branding, and color-coded status indicators (Exceeds Baseline / Progressing) with the stakeholder report slide design.
- [[concepts/tezino-camp-prep-spc-monitoring]] — SPC-based monitoring dashboard with first-class explainability requirements for coaching and medical staff; shares the "every metric needs a plain-language justification" communication principle and threshold-based flag logic.
- [[concepts/baylor-wtn-acwr-analysis]] — The dual-model (actual vs. compliant counterfactual) ACWR overlay is another athlete monitoring communication artifact designed to make statistical content interpretable for practitioners — the same decision-support framing used in the presentation.
- [[connections/athlete-monitoring-communication-grammar]] — The cross-cutting visual vocabulary (color coding, threshold flags, trend + flag + sentence) that independently recurs across the presentation, Zinnecker reports, Tezino SPC monitoring, and the Swiss Modern coaching deck.
- [[concepts/sports-coaching-slide-design-system]] — A parallel S&C coaching staff slide deck built the same day (Session 23:43) using the Swiss Modern preset; shares the traffic-light color constraint and HTML slide build context. The two projects together document complementary implementation gotchas: coaching deck (box-sizing, file:// URL mangling) and RTP presentation (synthetic keydown unreliability, dark-background CSS toggle, slide-8 chart overflow).
- [[concepts/rtp-clinic-deliverable-finalization]] — The parallel 31-slide Eric+Jeremy clinic deck; both efforts involve speaker-script restructuring, versioned deck files, and multi-viewport render verification, but this is the shorter single-author conference talk.

- [[daily/2026-06-17.md]] — Conference presentation design session (20:28): four design decisions locked, 11-slide running order established, Slide 9 stakeholder report format designed. Validation session (23:56): all 11 slides confirmed layout-clean at 1440×900 and 375×667, synthetic keydown unreliable, switched to dot-click navigation, dark-background Slide 11 visibility bug fixed via `on-dark` body class toggle.
- [[daily/2026-06-18.md]] — Speaker-script and duration session (01:12): full per-slide script saved to `RTP-Data-Collection-SCRIPT.md`, 11-slide deck measured at ~5–7 min vs 20-min slot, three substance-based gap-closure options framed. Versioning/bug-fix session (01:29): deck expanded to 14 slides (v2), original preserved as v1, slide-8 chart overflow fixed with `aspect-ratio` + `max-height: min(40vh, 320px)`.
